title: Software Discovery: Backup Software Discovery
summary: Backup Software Discovery is a targeted form of software enumeration aimed at the tools and configurations an organisation relies on to recover data. The adversary wants to know whether backups exist, where they are stored, whether they are currently reachable, and which product manages them, because that determines how much damage a destructive or encrypting payload can do. Typical products of interest include enterprise backup suites and popular consumer and small business tools, and enumeration looks much like other discovery: process and service listings, file system searches for product directories and repositories, registry queries for installed product keys and configuration, cloud API calls that list backup services and recovery points, and examination of mounted network shares or object storage buckets. Defenders should treat this as a high-value precursor, because it frequently appears shortly before data destruction or ransomware deployment. The strongest signals combine access to backup configuration or administration interfaces by an identity that has no backup duties, discovery commands executed from the same session that later stops or deletes recovery points, and sudden changes to backup catalogues, retention settings, or the availability of repository shares.

beginner.definition: This is an attacker hunting for the programs and storage that a company uses to back up its data. Backups are the copies that let you recover after a disaster. Finding them tells the attacker how much they can destroy and still leave you helpless.
beginner.whyItMatters: Good backups are the difference between a bad day and a lost company. If an attacker finds them, they can plan to delete or encrypt those copies first, so recovery becomes impossible. Backups are often stored on separate servers or in cloud storage, and those places may not be watched as closely as laptops. Seeing this search happen is one of the last clear warnings before data is destroyed.
howItWorks: The attacker already has a foothold and wants to know what recovery options exist.
They list running services and programs to identify backup products by name.
They search the disk for backup folders, stored catalogues and product configuration files.
They read the registry or the product settings files to learn backup schedules and storage locations.
They check network shares, cloud storage and account interfaces for backup copies.
They use what they learn to plan deleting or encrypting the copies before the main data.
beginner.example: Think of a family that keeps photocopies of important documents in a safe deposit box at the bank. A thief who plans to burn the house will first walk to the bank and check whether the box is guarded. Finding the copies is not the theft itself, but it decides how the theft will go.
takeaways: Attackers look for backups so they can remove your ability to recover.
Backup servers and cloud repositories need the same monitoring as endpoints.
Access to backup settings by staff without backup duties is a red flag.

objectives: Explain why adversaries specifically enumerate backup products and storage.
List host and cloud artefacts that reveal backup software and repositories.
Identify telemetry that shows unexpected access to backup configuration.
Link backup discovery to the destructive actions that often follow it.
Recommend backup protections such as offline copies and access separation.
